course.title: React Development
course.tagline: Build modern web apps with React, components, state and real data from an API.

days.title: What React Is and How to Set It Up
days.goal: Understand what React is and get a first React app running on your computer.

video.title: Learn React from Three All-Star Instructors

steps: Install Node.js from nodejs.org and check it with node -v in the terminal.
Create a React app with the Vite command: npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react.
Go into the folder, run npm install, then npm run dev.
Open the link in your browser and see the starter page.
days.task: Get the starter React app running and change the heading text to your name.
days.challenge: Change the starter page's heading, paragraph and button text to make it yours.

options: A JavaScript library for building user interfaces from small reusable pieces called components
quiz.explain: React is a library for building web pages out of components: small pieces that each handle one part of the page.

options: A fast tool that sets up and runs a React project
quiz.explain: Vite creates your project files and runs a fast development server so you can see changes instantly.

quiz.q: What does npm run dev do?
options: It starts the development server so you can view your app in the browser
quiz.explain: npm run dev starts the local server. You open its link in the browser to see your app.

days.title: Your First Component
days.goal: Understand components and build your first one.

video.title: Learn React JS in This Free 7-Hour Course

steps: Open src/App.jsx and find the App component function.
Make a new file Greeting.jsx with a function that returns an h1 with your name.
Import Greeting into App.jsx and use it like <Greeting />.
Run the app and check your greeting shows on the page.
days.task: Build three small components: a header, a welcome message and a footer, and show all three on the page.
days.challenge: Make a component that shows today's date inside a sentence.

options: A JavaScript function that returns what should appear on the page
quiz.explain: A component is a function that returns JSX, which describes a piece of the page.

options: A way to write HTML-like code inside JavaScript
quiz.explain: JSX looks like HTML but lives inside JavaScript. React turns it into real page elements.

quiz.q: How do you use a component in another file?
options: Export it from its file and import it where you need it
quiz.explain: You export the component from its file and import it in the file that needs it.

days.title: JSX Rules
days.goal: Write JSX correctly: one parent element, className and JavaScript inside curly braces.

video.title: Free React Course – 8 Real-World Projects and 140+ Coding Challenges

steps: Wrap two elements in one parent <div> or a fragment <>...</>.
Use className instead of class for CSS classes.
Put a JavaScript value inside JSX with curly braces, like {name}.
Write a comment inside JSX using {/* comment */}.
days.task: Build a profile card component that shows a name, age and city using variables in curly braces.
days.challenge: Make a component that shows the result of 5 + 3 inside a sentence using JSX.

quiz.q: Why must JSX return one parent element?
options: React needs a single root element to know where the component starts and ends
quiz.explain: A component returns one tree of elements, so everything must sit inside a single parent or fragment.

quiz.q: Why do we write className instead of class in JSX?
options: class is a reserved word in JavaScript, so React uses className
class does not work in CSS
quiz.explain: class is a JavaScript keyword, so JSX uses className for CSS classes.

quiz.q: What do curly braces do in JSX?
options: They let you run JavaScript and show its value
quiz.explain: Curly braces in JSX run JavaScript, so {name} shows the value of the name variable.

days.title: Props: Passing Data to Components
days.goal: Pass data into components with props so one component can show many things.

video.title: Learn React JS - Full Course for Beginners - Tutorial 2019

steps: Make a Card component that takes a title prop and shows it.
Use <Card title='Hello' /> and <Card title='Welcome' /> to show two different cards.
Pass a number prop like price={5000} and show it in the card.
Give a prop a default value so the card still works when no prop is given.
days.task: Build a product card component and use it to show three different products with different names and prices.
days.challenge: Make a Button component that takes a label prop and shows it on the button.

options: Data passed from a parent component to a child component
quiz.explain: Props are how a parent hands data to a child component, like passing arguments to a function.

quiz.q: How do you pass a number as a prop?
quiz.explain: Curly braces pass a JavaScript value. Quotes would pass the text '5000' instead of the number.

quiz.q: Can a child component change its own props?
options: No, props are read-only. The parent owns the data
quiz.explain: Props are read-only. If a value must change, it lives in state in the parent, not in props.

days.title: Rendering Lists
days.goal: Show a list of items on the page with map() and a key for each item.

video.title: Master React by Building 25 Projects

steps: Make an array of five names in your component.
Use names.map() to turn each name into an <li> element.
Give each <li> a key prop, like key={name}.
Show the list on the page and check all five names appear.
days.task: Show a list of five products with names and prices, each in its own card.
days.challenge: Add a button that adds a new item to the list and shows it on the page.

quiz.q: Why use map() to render a list?
options: It turns each item in an array into an element, one by one
quiz.explain: map() runs your function on every item and returns a new array, which React can render as elements.

quiz.q: What is the key prop for?
options: It helps React tell list items apart when the list changes
quiz.explain: Keys help React track which item is which when items are added, removed or reordered.

quiz.q: What should you use as a key?
options: A stable unique value, like an id or the item itself if unique
quiz.explain: Use a stable unique id. Random keys or indexes can confuse React when the list changes.

days.title: Conditional Rendering
days.goal: Show different things on the page based on a condition.

video.title: Comprehensive Full Stack React with Appwrite

steps: Use {isLoggedIn ? 'Welcome' : 'Please log in'} to show one of two messages.

Use {showDetails &&

Details here

} to show something only when true.
Make a boolean variable and flip it with a button to see the page change.
Show a loading message when data is not ready yet.
days.task: Build a page that shows 'You are logged in' or 'Please log in' based on a variable, with a button to switch.
days.challenge: Show a list only when it has items, otherwise show 'No items yet'.

quiz.q: What does {a ? b : c} do in JSX?
options: It shows b when a is true and c when a is false
quiz.explain: This is a ternary. It picks one of two values based on a condition.

options: It shows the paragraph only when show is true
quiz.explain: With &&, React renders the element only when the left side is true.

options: To show the right thing for the current state, like logged in or loading
quiz.explain: Pages change with state. Conditional rendering shows the right content for each situation.

days.title: Project 1: Personal Profile Page
days.goal: Build a profile page with several components, props and a list.

video.title: A Complete Guide to All React Hooks for Beginners

steps: Make Header, About, SkillsList and Footer components in separate files.
Pass your name and job title into the Header with props.
Show your skills as a list rendered with map() and keys.
Style the page with CSS so it looks like a real profile.
days.task: Finish the profile page with your real details and at least five skills.
days.challenge: Add a toggle button that shows or hides the About section.

quiz.q: Why split a page into components?
options: So each part is small, reusable and easy to fix
quiz.explain: Small components are easier to understand, test and reuse than one giant file.

quiz.q: What should a component file contain?
options: One component and its export, plus its own styles if needed
quiz.explain: One component per file keeps the project tidy and makes it easy to find things.

quiz.q: How do props help in a profile page?
options: They let the same card component show different people or skills
They make the page load faster
quiz.explain: Props let one component show many different values, so you reuse it instead of copying it.

project.title: Personal Profile Page
project.brief: Build a profile page in React with Header, About, SkillsList and Footer components, props for your details, a list rendered with map(), and a toggle that shows or hides the About section.
checks: The page is split into at least four components in separate files.
Your name and job title are passed in with props.
Your skills show as a list rendered with map() and keys.
A button toggles the About section on and off.
The page has CSS styling and looks like a real profile.
The app runs without errors in the browser.

days.title: useState: Your First Hook
days.goal: Add memory to a component with the useState hook.

video.title: All React Hooks Tutorial ( +Building Custom Hooks)

steps: Import useState from 'react' at the top of your file.
Make a count state with const [count, setCount] = useState(0).
Show count on the page and add a button that calls setCount(count + 1).
Click the button and watch the number grow without reloading.
days.task: Build a like button that shows a heart and a count that grows each time it is clicked.
days.challenge: Make a text input that shows what you type live on the page using state.

options: Data a component remembers and can change, which makes the page update
quiz.explain: State is data a component owns. When state changes, React re-renders the component with the new values.

options: An array with the current value and a function to change it
quiz.explain: useState returns [value, setValue]. You read the value and call the setter to change it.

quiz.q: Why must you use the setter instead of changing the variable directly?
options: Only the setter tells React to re-render with the new value
quiz.explain: Changing the variable directly does nothing on screen. The setter tells React to update the page.

days.title: Handling Events in React
days.goal: Handle clicks, typing and other events in React the right way.

video.title: React Hooks useState and useEffect Examples

steps: Add an onClick handler to a button that logs a message.
Pass the event object and log e.target to see which element was clicked.
Add an onChange handler to an input that updates state as you type.
Add an onSubmit handler to a form and stop the page reloading.
days.task: Build a small app with a button that changes a message and an input that updates a greeting live.
days.challenge: Make a button that counts double-clicks and shows the count.

quiz.q: How do you handle a click in React?
options: With an onClick prop that takes a function
quiz.explain: React uses props like onClick. You pass a function and React calls it when the event happens.

quiz.q: What is the event object e?
options: An object with details about the event, like which element was clicked
quiz.explain: React passes an event object to your handler. It carries details like the target element.

quiz.q: Why use onChange on an input instead of reading it later?
options: So state updates on every keystroke and the page can react live
quiz.explain: onChange keeps state in sync with what the user types, so the page can react instantly.

days.title: State with Objects and Arrays
days.goal: Keep state in objects and arrays and update them the right way.

video.title: Learn React JS - Full Beginner's Tutorial & Practice Projects

steps: Keep a user object in state and update one field with setUser({...user, age: 26}).
Keep a list in state and add an item with setList([...list, newItem]).
Remove an item with filter() and set the result as the new state.
Never change state directly: always make a new copy.
days.task: Build a form that stores name and email in one state object and shows them live.
days.challenge: Make a list where each item can be removed with a button.

options: To make a new object with the old values plus your change, without touching the old one
quiz.explain: React needs a new object to notice the change. Spreading copies the old values and adds your update.

quiz.q: What happens if you change state directly, like list.push(item)?
options: React may not notice the change and the page may not update
quiz.explain: React compares the old and new state. If you change the same object, it looks unchanged and may skip the update.

quiz.q: How do you remove an item from state?
options: Use filter() to make a new array without it and set that as state
quiz.explain: filter() returns a new array without the item. You set that new array as the new state.

days.title: Handling Forms
days.goal: Build forms that store every field in state.

video.title: Learn React by Building an eCommerce Site

steps: Make a form with a name input controlled by state.
Update the state on every keystroke with onChange.
Stop the form reloading the page with e.preventDefault() on submit.
Show the submitted data on the page after submit.
days.task: Build a sign-up form with name, email and password that shows a welcome message on submit.
days.challenge: Add a check that the email contains @ before accepting the form.

options: An input whose value comes from state and updates state on every keystroke
quiz.explain: A controlled input's value lives in state. You set value={state} and update it with onChange.

options: To stop the browser reloading the page so React can handle the data
quiz.explain: A form submit normally reloads the page. preventDefault() stops that so your code can handle it.

quiz.q: Where does form data live in React?
options: In state, so you can read it and check it any time
quiz.explain: Keeping form values in state lets you read, check and use them whenever you need.

days.title: useEffect: Side Effects
days.goal: Run code when a component loads or when a value changes, with useEffect.

video.title: The Best Way to Host & Deploy a React Application

steps: Import useEffect and run a console.log when the component first loads.
Fetch data from a public API inside useEffect and store it in state.
Add a dependency array [userId] so the effect runs again when userId changes.
Show a loading message while the data is being fetched.
days.task: Build a component that fetches a list of posts from a public API and shows their titles.
days.challenge: Add a clean-up that cancels a timer when the component unmounts.

options: Running code that touches the outside world, like fetching data or timers, at the right time
quiz.explain: useEffect runs side effects: fetching, timers, subscriptions. It runs after the component renders.

quiz.q: What does the dependency array do?
options: It lists the values that, when changed, make the effect run again
quiz.explain: React re-runs the effect only when a value in the dependency array changes.

quiz.q: What does an empty dependency array [] mean?
options: The effect runs once when the component first loads
The effect runs on every render
quiz.explain: An empty array means the effect has no dependencies, so it runs once after the first render.

days.title: Fetching Data from an API
days.goal: Load real data from an API and show it in your app.

video.title: Learn React from Three All-Star Instructors

steps: Use fetch() inside useEffect to get data from a public API.
Store the data in state with useState.
Show a loading message while waiting and an error message if it fails.
Render the data as a list of cards.
days.task: Build a users page that fetches users from a public API and shows each name and email in a card.
days.challenge: Add a search box that filters the fetched users by name.

options: So the fetch runs once when the component loads, not on every render
quiz.explain: Fetching in useEffect with an empty array runs once on load. Fetching during render would run again and again.

options: So the user sees 'Loading...' instead of a blank page while data arrives
quiz.explain: Data takes time to arrive. A loading state tells the user something is happening.

quiz.q: What should you do when the fetch fails?
options: Show a friendly error message and let the user try again
quiz.explain: A good app shows a clear error message and a way to retry instead of breaking.

days.title: Project 2: Todo App with React
days.goal: Build a full todo app with state, forms and local storage.

video.title: Learn React JS in This Free 7-Hour Course

steps: Make a form to add tasks and store them in state as an array.
Show the tasks as a list with a checkbox and a delete button for each.
Save tasks to localStorage whenever they change, and load them on start.
Add a filter: All, Active and Completed.
days.task: Finish the todo app with at least three tasks and test the filters.
days.challenge: Add a count that shows how many tasks are left to do.

options: So the tasks are still there after a page refresh
quiz.explain: State disappears on refresh. localStorage keeps the tasks in the browser between visits.

quiz.q: How do you save an array to localStorage?
options: Turn it into a JSON string with JSON.stringify() first
quiz.explain: localStorage only stores strings, so you stringify the array and parse it back when reading.

options: It shows only the tasks that match the chosen view: all, active or completed
quiz.explain: A filter picks which tasks to show based on their done state, without deleting anything.

project.title: Todo App with React
project.brief: Build a todo app in React: add tasks, check them off, delete them, filter by All/Active/Completed, and save them to localStorage so they survive a refresh.
checks: A form adds tasks to state as an array.
Each task has a checkbox and a delete button.
Checking a task marks it done and styles it differently.
Filters show All, Active or Completed tasks.
Tasks are saved to localStorage and loaded on start.
Empty tasks cannot be added.

days.title: Props Drilling and Lifting State
days.goal: Share state between components by lifting it to their common parent.

video.title: Free React Course – 8 Real-World Projects and 140+ Coding Challenges

steps: Put the state in the parent component that both children need.
Pass the value down as a prop to the child that shows it.
Pass the setter down as a prop to the child that changes it.
Check that clicking in one child updates what the other child shows.
days.task: Build a parent with two children: one shows a count, the other has buttons to change it.
days.challenge: Lift a search box state to the parent so a list in another child can be filtered.

options: Moving state to the nearest common parent so two children can share it
quiz.explain: When two children need the same data, the state lives in their parent and is passed down as props.

options: Passing a prop through several layers of components that do not need it, just to reach a deep child
quiz.explain: Prop drilling is passing data through middle components that only forward it. It works but gets messy in big apps.

quiz.q: How does a child change parent state?
options: The parent passes the setter function down as a prop and the child calls it
quiz.explain: The parent passes setCount down as a prop. The child calls it, and the parent's state changes.

days.title: Debugging React with DevTools
days.goal: Find and fix problems using React DevTools in the browser.

video.title: Learn React JS - Full Course for Beginners - Tutorial 2019

steps: Install the React DevTools browser extension.
Open the Components tab and inspect your component tree.
Click a component to see its props and state live.
Change a prop value in DevTools and watch the page update.
days.task: Use DevTools to find why a list is not showing, then fix the bug.
days.challenge: Use the Profiler tab to see which components render when you type.

quiz.q: What does React DevTools show you?
options: Your component tree with each component's props and state
quiz.explain: DevTools shows your components as a tree. You can inspect props, state and hooks for each one.

quiz.q: What is the Profiler tab for?
options: Seeing which components render and how long each render takes
quiz.explain: The Profiler records renders and shows which components were slow, so you know what to optimise.

options: To check what data a component actually received, which finds many bugs fast
quiz.explain: Most React bugs are wrong data. Seeing the actual props shows you what went wrong.

days.title: Styling React Apps
days.goal: Style your app with CSS files, modules and simple inline styles.

video.title: Master React by Building 25 Projects

steps: Import a CSS file into a component and use className to apply it.
Make a button style with a hover effect in CSS.
Try inline styles with a JavaScript object, like style={{ color: 'red' }}.
Use a CSS module so class names do not clash between components.
days.task: Style your todo app: give it a clean card layout, colours and spacing.
days.challenge: Make the app look good on a phone screen with a media query.

quiz.q: How do you add CSS to a React component?
options: Import a CSS file at the top of the component file
quiz.explain: You import './App.css' in the component file and use className to apply the classes.

options: A CSS file that is global
A CSS file whose class names are scoped to one component
quiz.explain: CSS modules scope class names to the component that imports them, so names never clash.

options: For small dynamic styles that depend on state, like a colour that changes
quiz.explain: Inline styles are handy when a style value depends on state, but big styles belong in CSS files.

days.title: React Router: Pages in One App
days.goal: Add pages to your app with React Router.

video.title: Comprehensive Full Stack React with Appwrite

steps: Install react-router-dom with npm install react-router-dom.
Wrap your app in <BrowserRouter> and define Routes.
Make Home, About and Contact pages as components.
Link between pages with <Link> instead of <a> so the page does not reload.
days.task: Add three pages to your todo app project: Home, Todos and About, with navigation links.
days.challenge: Add a page for a single todo that shows its details by id.

options: A library that lets one React app have many pages with different URLs
quiz.explain: React Router maps URLs to components, so your app feels like many pages without reloading.

options: <Link> changes the page without a full reload, keeping your state
quiz.explain: A normal link reloads the whole page and loses state. <Link> swaps the component in place.

options: A part of the URL, like /todo/3, that you read to show one item
quiz.explain: Route parameters let one page component show different items based on the id in the URL.

days.title: Custom Hooks
days.goal: Write your own hooks to reuse logic across components.

video.title: A Complete Guide to All React Hooks for Beginners

steps: Make a file useLocalStorage.js that stores a value in localStorage.
Use it in two different components to share the same logic.
Name your hook with 'use' at the start, like useFetch.
Make a useFetch hook that fetches a URL and returns data and loading.
days.task: Write a useDocumentTitle hook that sets the page title, and use it in two pages.
days.challenge: Replace the todo app's localStorage code with your useLocalStorage hook.

options: A function starting with 'use' that reuses hook logic across components
quiz.explain: A custom hook is a function that uses built-in hooks inside it, so you can reuse that logic anywhere.

quiz.q: Why must hook names start with 'use'?
options: React uses the 'use' prefix to recognise hooks and check their rules
quiz.explain: The 'use' prefix tells React and its tools that the function is a hook, so its rules apply.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of a custom hook?
options: You write logic once and reuse it in many components
quiz.explain: Custom hooks stop you copying the same logic into many components.

days.title: Context: Sharing Data Without Drilling
days.goal: Share data across many components with Context.

video.title: All React Hooks Tutorial ( +Building Custom Hooks)

steps: Create a context with createContext() and a provider component.
Wrap your app in the provider and pass a value to it.
Read the value in a deep child with useContext().
Use context for a theme (light/dark) that many components need.
days.task: Add a dark mode toggle to your app using context, so any component can read the theme.
days.challenge: Move your user data into context so the header and profile page can both read it.

options: A way to share data with many components without passing props through every layer
quiz.explain: Context lets you provide a value at the top and read it in any deep child, skipping prop drilling.

options: For data many components need, like theme, user or language
quiz.explain: Context fits global data like theme or the logged-in user. Local data should stay in local state.

options: It reads the nearest provider's value for a context
quiz.explain: useContext() returns the value provided by the closest provider above the component.

days.title: Project 3: Shop or Blog App
days.goal: Build a bigger app with pages, data fetching and state.

video.title: React Hooks useState and useEffect Examples

steps: Plan the app: pages, components and what data each needs.
Fetch a list of products or posts from a public API and show them as cards.
Add a detail page that shows one item when clicked.
Add a cart or favourites feature using state and context.
days.task: Finish the shop or blog app with at least 8 items and a working detail page.
days.challenge: Add a search box that filters the items by name.

quiz.q: Why plan before building a bigger app?
options: So you know the pages, components and data flow before you start writing code
quiz.explain: A small plan stops you getting lost. You know what to build and in what order.

quiz.q: How do pages and components fit together?
options: Pages are components that hold other components for one URL
quiz.explain: A page is just a component for one route. It is built from smaller components like cards and lists.

options: In context or a parent, so the header and the cart page can both read it
quiz.explain: Shared state like a cart belongs high up, in context or a parent, so every part of the app can reach it.

project.title: Shop or Blog App
project.brief: Build a shop or blog app: fetch at least 8 products or posts from a public API, show them as cards, add a detail page for one item, and add a cart or favourites feature.
checks: The app fetches at least 8 items from a public API.
Items show as cards with a name, price or summary.
Clicking an item opens a detail page for it.
A cart or favourites feature works with state or context.
A search box filters the items by name.
The app has navigation between pages.

days.title: Forms and Validation
days.goal: Build forms with validation that tells users what to fix.

video.title: Learn React JS - Full Beginner's Tutorial & Practice Projects

steps: Keep each field in state and show an error message under a bad field.
Check the email contains @ and the password is at least 8 characters.
Disable the submit button until the form is valid.
Show a success message when the form is submitted correctly.
days.task: Build a registration form with name, email and password validation.
days.challenge: Add a rule that the two password fields must match.

options: In state, so they can show under the right field
quiz.explain: Errors in state let you show them next to the field and clear them when the user fixes it.

options: On submit and, for a better feel, as the user types or leaves a field
quiz.explain: Validating on submit is required. Validating as the user types gives faster feedback.

quiz.q: Why disable the submit button until the form is valid?
options: To stop invalid data being sent and to show clearly what is missing
quiz.explain: A disabled button prevents bad submissions and signals that something still needs fixing.

days.title: Error Boundaries
days.goal: Stop one broken component from crashing your whole app.

video.title: Learn React by Building an eCommerce Site

steps: Make a class component called ErrorBoundary with getDerivedStateFromError.
Wrap a risky component in the boundary.
Make the boundary show a friendly message when a child crashes.
Log the error in componentDidCatch for debugging.
days.task: Wrap your shop app's detail page in an error boundary and test it with a bad item id.
days.challenge: Add a 'Try again' button to the error message that resets the boundary.

options: A component that catches JavaScript errors in its children and shows a fallback instead of crashing the whole app
quiz.explain: An error boundary catches errors in the components below it and shows a friendly message instead of a blank page.

quiz.q: Why use a class component for an error boundary?
options: React only supports error boundaries as class components
quiz.explain: Error boundaries must be class components. There is no hook version yet.

options: A clear message that something went wrong and a way to try again
quiz.explain: A good fallback explains the problem in plain words and offers a way forward.

days.title: Performance Basics
days.goal: Keep your app fast with memo, useMemo and useCallback.

video.title: The Best Way to Host & Deploy a React Application

steps: Wrap a slow child component in React.memo so it skips renders when props do not change.
Use useMemo to avoid recalculating an expensive value on every render.
Use useCallback to keep a function the same between renders.
Check in React DevTools which components re-render when you type.
days.task: Find a component in your app that renders too often and wrap it in memo.
days.challenge: Use useMemo to cache a filtered list so it only recalculates when the list changes.

options: It skips re-rendering a component when its props have not changed
It makes components faster to load
quiz.explain: memo compares the new props with the old ones. If nothing changed, React reuses the last render.

options: It remembers a calculated value and only recalculates it when its dependencies change
quiz.explain: useMemo caches an expensive calculation so it only runs again when its inputs change.

options: Only when you can see a real slowdown, not before
quiz.explain: Optimising too early adds complexity. Measure first, then optimise the slow parts.

days.title: Testing React Components
days.goal: Test your components so you can change them with confidence.

video.title: Learn React from Three All-Star Instructors

steps: Install a testing setup and write a test that renders a component.
Check that a heading with the right text appears on the page.
Simulate a button click and check the count changes.
Run the tests and read the pass and fail results.
days.task: Write tests for your like button and your todo list add function.
days.challenge: Write a test that checks an error message appears for bad form input.

options: A test that renders a component and checks it shows and behaves correctly
quiz.explain: Component tests render your component, check what it shows, and simulate clicks to check it behaves.

options: So you can change code safely, knowing tests will catch breaks
quiz.explain: Tests catch regressions. When you refactor, green tests tell you nothing broke.

options: The important behaviour: what shows, what happens on click, what happens on bad input
quiz.explain: Test the behaviour users care about first: what appears, what clicks do, and what errors show.

days.title: Deploying Your React App
days.goal: Build your app for production and put it on the internet.

video.title: Learn React JS in This Free 7-Hour Course

steps: Run npm run build to create the production files.
Check the dist folder and the size of the built files.
Deploy the folder to Netlify with drag and drop.
Open the live link on your phone and check the app works.
days.task: Deploy your shop or blog app and share the live link with one person.
days.challenge: Fix any issue that only appears in the built version, like a wrong image path.

quiz.q: What does npm run build do?
options: It creates optimised production files in the dist folder
quiz.explain: build bundles and minifies your code into small production files ready to host.

quiz.q: Why check the live site on your phone?
options: Because real users visit on phones, and problems like layout or touch issues show up there
quiz.explain: Testing on a real phone catches layout and touch problems you miss on a desktop.

options: A way to deploy a folder by dragging it onto the Netlify site
quiz.explain: Netlify Drop lets you publish a built folder by dragging it in, with no setup.

days.title: State Management with a Reducer
days.goal: Manage complex state with useReducer instead of many useState calls.

video.title: Free React Course – 8 Real-World Projects and 140+ Coding Challenges

steps: Define a reducer function that handles 'add', 'remove' and 'clear' actions.
Use useReducer to get state and a dispatch function.
Send actions with dispatch({ type: 'add', item }) from your buttons.
Check the state updates correctly for each action.
days.task: Rewrite your todo app's state with useReducer.
days.challenge: Add a 'toggle' action that marks a task done or not done.

options: A function that takes the current state and an action and returns the new state
quiz.explain: A reducer is a pure function: (state, action) => newState. It describes every way state can change.

quiz.q: When is useReducer better than useState?
options: When state has many related values or many ways to change
quiz.explain: useReducer fits complex state with many transitions, like a cart or a form, better than many useState calls.

options: The function you call with an action to ask the reducer to update state
quiz.explain: dispatch sends an action to the reducer, which returns the new state and triggers a re-render.

days.title: Code Splitting and Lazy Loading
days.goal: Load pages only when users need them so your app starts faster.

video.title: Learn React JS - Full Course for Beginners - Tutorial 2019

steps: Import a page with React.lazy() instead of a normal import.
Wrap it in <Suspense> with a loading message as the fallback.
Split each route into its own lazy chunk.
Check the network tab to see chunks loading only when you visit a page.
days.task: Lazy-load the About and Contact pages in your app and check they load on demand.
days.challenge: Measure the first load size before and after lazy loading.

options: Breaking your app into smaller files that load only when needed
quiz.explain: Code splitting breaks your bundle into chunks. Each chunk loads only when the user visits that part.

options: It loads a component only when it is first rendered
quiz.explain: lazy() delays loading a component until it is needed, which makes the first load faster.

options: Showing a fallback, like 'Loading...', while a lazy component loads
quiz.explain: Suspense wraps lazy components and shows your fallback while the code is still downloading.

days.title: Polish and Accessibility
days.goal: Make your app usable for everyone, including keyboard and screen reader users.

video.title: Master React by Building 25 Projects

steps: Use real <button> elements instead of clickable divs.
Add labels to every form input with htmlFor.
Check colour contrast and make sure text is readable.
Test your app using only the keyboard: Tab to move, Enter to activate.
days.task: Fix the accessibility issues in your shop app: labels, buttons and focus styles.
days.challenge: Add alt text to every image in your app.

options: Buttons work with keyboards and screen readers by default, divs do not
quiz.explain: Real buttons are focusable and announce themselves to screen readers. A div with onClick is not.

quiz.q: What does a label do for an input?
options: It tells screen readers and users what the input is for, and clicking it focuses the input
quiz.explain: Labels link text to inputs, so assistive tech can announce them and users can click the label to focus.

options: Making apps usable by everyone, including people with disabilities
quiz.explain: Accessibility means people using keyboards, screen readers or other tools can still use your app fully.

days.title: Capstone Prep: Plan Your App
days.goal: Review everything, pick your capstone app and plan your demo.

video.title: Comprehensive Full Stack React with Appwrite

steps: List all the apps you built in 30 days and pick your favourite.
Write a short plan: the problem, the pages, the components and the data.
Practise explaining your app in simple words, as if to a friend.
Record a short video or write a short post showing your app running.
days.task: Write your capstone plan and a one-minute explanation of your app.
days.challenge: Show your app to one person and note their questions, then improve your explanation.

quiz.q: What makes a good capstone app?
options: One real problem solved well, with clean code and a working demo
quiz.explain: A good capstone solves one real problem clearly, with clean code and a demo that works.

options: Because explaining simply proves you truly understand it
quiz.explain: If you can explain your code in simple words, you really understand it. That is what employers look for.

quiz.q: What should your capstone plan include?
options: The problem, the pages, the components, the data and how you will show it
quiz.explain: A plan covers the problem, the pages and components, the data source and how you will present it.

capstone.title: Build and Share a Complete React App
capstone.brief: Build a complete React app that solves a real problem: a budget tracker, a study planner, a recipe book or a small shop. It must have at least three pages with React Router, data from a public API, state with hooks, and a clean design. Deploy it live and share the link with a README and a short demo.
checks: The app solves one real problem and you can explain the problem in one sentence.
It has at least three pages with React Router and navigation.
It fetches real data from a public API and shows loading and error states.
It uses useState and useEffect, plus one more hook like useContext or a custom hook.
Data the user creates is saved in localStorage.
It is deployed live with a README that explains how to use it.
You can show a live demo and explain how it works in simple words.
deliverables: A live deployed link to the app.
A README.md explaining the problem, the features and how to use it.
A short demo video or screenshots showing the app running.
A one-page write-up of what you learned in 30 days.
